title: Idioms & Phrases
intro: An idiom is a phrase whose meaning can't be guessed from the individual words — 'a piece of cake' means something easy, not a dessert. SSC gives an idiom and asks for its meaning (or the reverse). Because the meaning is non-literal, you have to learn each idiom; the good news is that the same few hundred recur, and many group into themes (money, time, difficulty).

items.name: Use context if given
items.formula: how the idiom sits in the sentence hints at sense

items.name: Group by theme
items.formula: money, time, anger, success — learn in clusters

items.name: Phrasal verbs
items.formula: verb + particle changes meaning (give up, give in)

topics.name: Common Idioms
topics.details: Learn the meaning of each high-frequency idiom as a unit. Don't translate word by word — recall the whole-phrase meaning.

solved.problem: Meaning of "once in a blue moon".
Meaning of "hit the nail on the head".

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "cost an arm and a leg".
Meaning of "break the ice".
unsolved.answer: To start a conversation / ease tension

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "burn the midnight oil".
unsolved.answer: To work/study late into the night

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "bite the bullet".
Meaning of "let the cat out of the bag".

topics.name: Phrasal Verbs
topics.details: A phrasal verb is a verb plus a particle whose combination has a special meaning. The same verb changes meaning with different particles: 'give up' = quit, 'give in' = surrender, 'give away' = donate/reveal.

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "give in".
Meaning of "run out of".
Meaning of "carry out".
Meaning of "turn down".
Meaning of "bring up".
unsolved.answer: To raise (a child or a topic)

topics.name: Proverbs
topics.details: A proverb is a short, well-known saying that states a general truth or advice. SSC asks the meaning or the matching situation.

solved.problem: Meaning of "A stitch in time saves nine".
solved.solution: Timely action prevents bigger problems later.

solved.problem: Meaning of "Too many cooks spoil the broth".
solved.solution: Too many people working on one task ruin it.

solved.problem: Meaning of "Where there's a will, there's a way".
solved.solution: Determination finds a way to succeed.

solved.problem: Meaning of "Don't count your chickens before they hatch".
solved.solution: Don't assume success before it happens.

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "Make hay while the sun shines".
unsolved.answer: Use an opportunity while it lasts

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "A rolling stone gathers no moss".
Meaning of "Birds of a feather flock together".
unsolved.answer: Similar people associate with each other

unsolved.problem: Meaning of "Look before you leap".
Meaning of "Actions speak louder than words".
unsolved.answer: What you do matters more than what you say

topics.name: Idioms in Context
topics.details: When an idiom appears inside a sentence, the surrounding words confirm its meaning — use them. In the substitution format, replace the idiom with its plain meaning and check the sentence still makes sense.

solved.problem: "He passed the exam without studying — it was a piece of cake." Meaning of the idiom here?
"She finally spilled the beans about the surprise." Meaning?
"They had to bite the bullet and pay the fine." Meaning?
"The new phone cost an arm and a leg." Meaning?

unsolved.problem: "Let's break the ice with a quick game." Meaning?
unsolved.answer: To ease initial tension / start interaction

unsolved.problem: "He burns the midnight oil before exams." Meaning?
"Don't let the cat out of the bag." Meaning?
"We see him once in a blue moon." Meaning?
"She hit the nail on the head." Meaning?

shortcuts: Never read an idiom literally — the meaning is figurative.
Use the sentence context to confirm the sense when it is given.
Learn idioms in themed clusters (money, time, difficulty).
Phrasal verbs: the particle changes everything (give up / give in / give away).
In substitution, swap the idiom for its plain meaning and check it fits.
mistakes: Interpreting an idiom word by word.
Confusing close phrasal verbs (give up vs give in).
Picking a literal-sounding option over the true figurative meaning.
Ignoring sentence context that disambiguates the idiom.
pyq: SSC asks 1–3 idiom/phrase meanings per Tier 1, often as "choose the meaning of the underlined idiom". The set repeats, so drilling the common idioms and phrasal verbs pays off directly.
summary: Idioms and proverbs are non-literal and must be learned as whole units; phrasal verbs change meaning with their particle. Drill the high-frequency set in themed clusters, use sentence context to confirm sense, and in substitution swap the idiom for its plain meaning to check the fit.
